title: Tracing & Observability (LangSmith, Langfuse, OTel)
summary: You can't debug or evaluate what you can't see. Tracing captures every LLM call and tool invocation in an agent run as a span — with its inputs, outputs, token counts, and latency — and nests those spans into a tree that mirrors the run's control flow. Tools like LangSmith, Langfuse, and OpenTelemetry differ in APIs, but the durable concepts are the same: traces, spans, parent/child context, and attributes. Learn the concepts and the SDK churn stops mattering.
nestedConcepts: spans as the unit of observability
the trace tree of a run

subtopics.title: A span is one recorded operation
subtopics.explanation: A span captures a single unit of work — one LLM call, one tool invocation, one retrieval — recording when it started and ended plus its inputs, outputs, and metadata. It is the atom of observability: everything you later inspect, aggregate, or evaluate is built from spans. Getting the span boundary right (one operation per span) is what makes a trace readable instead of a soup of overlapping timings.
subtopics.example:
import time

class Span:
    def __init__(self, name, inputs):
        self.name, self.inputs = name, inputs
        self.start = time.time()
        self.outputs = None
    def end(self, outputs, **attrs):
        self.outputs = outputs
        self.latency_ms = (time.time() - self.start) * 1000
        self.attrs = attrs   # tokens, cost, model, ...

span = Span("llm.call", {"prompt": "hi"})
span.end({"text": "hello"}, tokens=12, model="gpt-x")
print(span.name, span.latency_ms is not None, span.attrs["tokens"])

subtopics.title: The trace tree mirrors the run
subtopics.explanation: A trace is the whole agent run, and its spans nest into a tree: the top-level run span contains a planner LLM span, which contains the tool spans it triggered, which may contain nested retrieval or sub-agent spans. Reading the tree top-down shows you exactly what the agent decided and in what order. This hierarchy is what turns a flat log of calls into a story you can actually follow.

subtopics.title: Context propagation links parent to child
subtopics.explanation: Spans only nest correctly if each new span knows its parent, which is carried in a trace context that must be threaded through every call — across function boundaries, threads, and async tasks. If the context isn't propagated, a child span attaches to the root (or nothing) and appears orphaned, breaking the tree. Correct propagation is the single most fragile and important part of tracing, and it's where most real bugs live.
subtopics.example:
import contextvars

current_span = contextvars.ContextVar("current_span", default=None)

def start_span(name):
    parent = current_span.get()          # read the active parent
    span = {"name": name, "parent": parent}
    token = current_span.set(span)       # this span is now the parent
    return span, token

run, t1 = start_span("agent.run")
plan, t2 = start_span("llm.plan")        # parent = agent.run, correctly
print(plan["parent"]["name"])            # agent.run

subtopics.title: Attributes carry tokens, latency, and cost
subtopics.explanation: Beyond structure, each span records attributes — the model name, prompt and completion token counts, latency, computed cost, and any custom tags. These are what you aggregate across a run or across production to find the slow, expensive, or failing steps. Rich, consistent attributes are what let observability answer 'where is the cost and latency going?' instead of just 'what happened?'.
subtopics.example:
def annotate(span, usage, model, price_per_1k):
    span["model"] = model
    span["prompt_tokens"] = usage["prompt"]
    span["completion_tokens"] = usage["completion"]
    total = usage["prompt"] + usage["completion"]
    # cost is derived from token counts and the model's price
    span["cost_usd"] = round(total / 1000 * price_per_1k, 6)
    return span

s = annotate({}, {"prompt": 800, "completion": 200}, "gpt-x", 0.01)
print(s["cost_usd"])   # 0.01

subtopics.title: Concepts outlive the SDK
subtopics.explanation: LangSmith, Langfuse, and OpenTelemetry expose the same primitives — trace, span, parent context, attributes — behind different decorators and clients, and those APIs change often. If you internalize the concepts and wrap the vendor SDK behind a thin adapter of your own, a breaking release or a switch of vendor is a small edit, not a rewrite. Investing in the durable model rather than a specific API is what keeps your instrumentation from rotting.

foundations.overview: An agent run is a branching sequence of LLM calls and tool invocations, and when something is slow, expensive, or wrong, a plain text log rarely tells you which step is to blame. Tracing fixes this by recording each operation as a span — its inputs, outputs, token usage, latency, and cost — and nesting spans into a trace tree that mirrors the run's control flow, so you can read top-down exactly what the agent decided and where the time and money went. The mechanism that makes the tree correct is context propagation: every span must know its parent, carried in a trace context that has to be threaded across function calls, threads, and async boundaries; when that context isn't propagated, spans orphan and the tree falls apart. Vendors — LangSmith, Langfuse, and OpenTelemetry among them — package these ideas behind different decorators and clients that churn frequently, but the underlying concepts (trace, span, parent/child context, attributes) are stable. If you learn the concepts and hide the vendor behind a thin adapter, SDK breakage becomes a one-file edit. Observability built this way is the foundation for debugging, cost control, and every form of production evaluation that samples real traces.
foundations.formalDefinition: A span is a timed record of a single operation with inputs, outputs, and attributes (model, tokens, latency, cost). A trace is the tree of spans for one end-to-end run, connected by parent/child relationships carried in a propagated trace context. Observability tooling (LangSmith, Langfuse, OpenTelemetry) captures, stores, and visualizes these traces; the concepts are vendor-independent even though the SDK APIs differ.
foundations.whyItMatters: Agents fail in ways a stack trace can't explain — a wrong tool choice, a bloated prompt, a slow retrieval buried three levels deep. Span-level traces make the invisible visible, which is the prerequisite for debugging, attributing cost and latency, and sampling production runs for online evaluation.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a trace as a call stack you can see after the fact, drawn as a tree: the run is the root, each LLM/tool call is a node with timing and I/O, and parent/child edges show who invoked whom. Context propagation is the thread that stitches a child onto the right parent; drop the thread and the child floats off as an orphan.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Engineers open a trace to see why an agent picked the wrong tool, aggregate span attributes to find the token-heaviest prompt, watch p95 latency per tool in production, and sample real traces to feed an online judge — all built on the same span/tree/context primitives regardless of vendor.
foundations.performanceImpact: Instrumentation adds small per-span overhead (timing, serialization, and export), usually negligible against model latency, but capturing full inputs/outputs on every span can dominate storage and network; teams sample traces, truncate large payloads, and export asynchronously so tracing doesn't slow the hot path.
commonUseCases: Debugging why an agent chose the wrong tool or answer
Attributing token cost and latency to specific spans
Monitoring p95 latency and error rate per tool in prod
Sampling real traces to feed online evaluation/judging

commonMisconceptions.myth: Logging print statements is basically the same as tracing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Logs are flat and unstructured; tracing records timed, nested spans with typed attributes and parent/child links, so you can see the tree and aggregate tokens/latency/cost — which flat logs can't give you.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Adding a tracing decorator once instruments the whole agent.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Spans only nest correctly if the trace context is propagated across every call, thread, and async boundary. Miss the propagation and child spans orphan even though the decorator ran.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Switching from LangSmith to Langfuse (or OTel) means rewriting your instrumentation.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The concepts — trace, span, parent context, attributes — are identical across vendors. Behind a thin adapter, a vendor switch is a small edit, not a rewrite.

interactiveExamples.title: Build a minimal span with I/O, tokens, and latency
interactiveExamples.explanation: A span is just a timed record of one operation plus its attributes. This tiny context-manager span captures inputs, outputs, token count, and latency — the same fields every tracing SDK records under different names.

code.caption: The context manager stamps latency automatically on exit; you fill in outputs and attributes inside — exactly the shape a real span exports.

interactiveExamples.title: Nesting spans into a trace tree via propagated context
interactiveExamples.explanation: Spans nest correctly only when each new span reads the current active span as its parent from a propagated context. This builds a small trace tree and prints the parent of each span to prove the hierarchy is right.

code.code:
import contextvars
from contextlib import contextmanager

current = contextvars.ContextVar("current", default=None)
SPANS = []

@contextmanager
def span(name):
    parent = current.get()                 # inherit the active parent
    rec = {"name": name, "parent": parent["name"] if parent else None}
    SPANS.append(rec)
    token = current.set(rec)               # become the parent for children
    try:
        yield rec
    finally:
        current.reset(token)               # restore parent on exit

with span("agent.run"):
    with span("llm.plan"):
        with span("tool.search"):
            pass
    with span("llm.answer"):
        pass

for s in SPANS:
    print(f"{s['name']:12} parent={s['parent']}")
code.caption: Each span reads its parent from the context var and restores it on exit, so tool.search nests under llm.plan while llm.answer sits directly under the run — a correct tree.
code.expectedOutput:
agent.run    parent=None
llm.plan     parent=agent.run
tool.search  parent=llm.plan
llm.answer   parent=agent.run

codeLab.title: Implement a context-propagating tracer
codeLab.instructions: Complete the Tracer class so spans nest into a correct tree. Implement span(name) as a context manager that: (1) reads the currently-active span from a contextvars.ContextVar as the new span's parent, (2) appends a record {'name', 'parent', 'children': []} to self.spans and to its parent's children list if a parent exists, (3) sets the context var so nested spans see this span as their parent, and (4) resets the context var on exit so siblings get the right parent. self.spans should end up containing every span in creation order. Complete the class so the harness passes.
codeLab.testHarness:
t = Tracer()
with t.span("agent.run") as run:
    with t.span("llm.plan"):
        with t.span("tool.search"):
            pass
    with t.span("llm.answer"):
        pass

names = [s["name"] for s in t.spans]
assert names == ["agent.run", "llm.plan", "tool.search", "llm.answer"]

by = {s["name"]: s for s in t.spans}
assert by["agent.run"]["parent"] is None
assert by["llm.plan"]["parent"] == "agent.run"
assert by["tool.search"]["parent"] == "llm.plan"
assert by["llm.answer"]["parent"] == "agent.run"
assert [c["name"] for c in run["children"]] == ["llm.plan", "llm.answer"]
print("all tests passed")
hints: Use self._current.get() at the top of span() to grab the parent before you create the new record.
Append the new record to parent['children'] only when a parent exists, then always append it to self.spans for creation order.
Save the token from self._current.set(rec) and call self._current.reset(token) in a finally block so siblings don't inherit a stale parent.

debuggingLab.title: Spans orphaned because trace context isn't propagated across a step
debuggingLab.symptom: In the tracing UI, the top-level agent.run span shows only the planner LLM span as a child; the tool spans that the planner triggered appear as separate, parentless root traces instead of nesting under the run. Latency and cost roll-ups are wrong because the tool work isn't attributed to the run, and the trace tree is unreadable.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The span machinery is correct, but the context is lost at a thread boundary. contextvars are copied into a thread only if you explicitly carry them; a bare threading.Thread starts with a fresh, default context, so inside run_tool the ContextVar 'current' reads its default (None). Each tool span therefore records parent=None and becomes an orphan root instead of nesting under llm.plan. Nothing errors — the tree is just silently wrong, which is exactly the failure mode that breaks latency/cost roll-ups.
commonMistakes: Assuming contextvars automatically flow into threads — they don't; a new thread gets a default context unless you copy the current one.
Only decorating functions with @span and never verifying the parent links, so orphaned spans go unnoticed until roll-ups look wrong.
Fixing it by stashing the parent in a global instead of propagating context, which breaks under concurrency and async where multiple runs interleave.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the tool spans nest under llm.plan even though they run on worker threads. Propagate the active context into each thread (capture it on the parent and run the worker inside that copied context) so the ContextVar resolves to the real parent instead of the default.

solution.code:
import contextvars, threading
from contextlib import contextmanager

current = contextvars.ContextVar("current", default=None)
SPANS = []

@contextmanager
def span(name):
    parent = current.get()
    rec = {"name": name, "parent": parent["name"] if parent else None}
    SPANS.append(rec)
    token = current.set(rec)
    try:
        yield rec
    finally:
        current.reset(token)

def run_tool(name):
    with span(name):
        pass

with span("agent.run"):
    with span("llm.plan"):
        threads = []
        for i in range(2):
            # capture the CURRENT context (which has llm.plan active)
            ctx = contextvars.copy_context()
            # run the worker inside that context so 'current' resolves
            # to llm.plan instead of the thread's default (None)
            th = threading.Thread(target=ctx.run,
                                  args=(run_tool, f"tool.{i}"))
            threads.append(th)
        for th in threads: th.start()
        for th in threads: th.join()

for s in SPANS:
    print(s["name"], "-> parent", s["parent"])

checkpoints.prompt: What is a span in agent tracing?
options: The entire agent run from start to finish
A timed record of one operation (an LLM or tool call) with its inputs, outputs, and attributes
A log line printed to stdout
The system prompt sent to the model
checkpoints.explanation: A span is the atom of observability: one unit of work with timing, I/O, and attributes like tokens and cost. Many spans nest into a trace, which represents the whole run.

checkpoints.prompt: Why do child spans sometimes appear orphaned (attached to no parent)?
options: The trace context (parent) wasn't propagated across a function, thread, or async boundary
The vendor SDK is out of date
checkpoints.explanation: Nesting depends on each span knowing its parent via a propagated trace context. If that context isn't carried across a boundary, the child reads the default (no parent) and orphans, silently breaking the tree.

checkpoints.prompt: Using a contextvars-based tracer, what parent does the inner span record?
checkpoints.explanation: start('run') sets 'run' as the active span; start('plan') then reads it as the parent, so plan's parent is the run span and its name is 'run'.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the line that carries the active trace context into a worker thread so spans don't orphan.
checkpoints.explanation: contextvars.copy_context() snapshots the current context (with the parent span active); running the worker via ctx.run makes the ContextVar resolve to the real parent instead of the thread's default.

theory.question: Explain traces, spans, and context propagation, and why the concepts matter more than the specific SDK.
theory.directAnswer: A span is a timed record of one operation (an LLM or tool call) with inputs, outputs, and attributes like tokens, latency, and cost; a trace is the tree of spans for one end-to-end run, connected by parent/child links carried in a propagated context. LangSmith, Langfuse, and OpenTelemetry expose these same primitives behind different APIs, so learning the concepts — and hiding the vendor behind an adapter — makes SDK churn a non-issue.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A structured, hierarchical record of an agent run: spans as nodes, a trace as the tree, and attributes as the per-span data you aggregate.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Agents branch across many LLM/tool calls and fail in ways stack traces can't explain, so you need timed, nested, attributed records to see where behavior, cost, and latency come from.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each operation opens a span that reads the active span as its parent from a propagated context, records I/O and attributes, and closes with a duration; spans nest into a trace you can read top-down and aggregate across.

theory.whyImportant: Span-level traces are the prerequisite for debugging wrong tool choices, attributing cost/latency, and sampling production runs for evaluation — none of which flat logs support.
theory.realWorldExample: A p95 latency spike was traced to a retriever span nested three levels under a tool call; the tree made the culprit obvious where a flat log would have buried it.

followUps.question: How do you keep instrumentation vendor-independent?
followUps.answer: Wrap the SDK behind a thin Tracer adapter exposing your own span() interface, so a vendor or version change edits one file instead of every call site.

followUps.question: What's the difference between a trace and a span?
followUps.answer: A span is one operation; a trace is the whole run — the tree of all spans linked by parent/child context.

theory.question: What is context propagation and why is it the most fragile part of tracing?
theory.directAnswer: Context propagation is threading the active trace context (the current parent span) through every call so new spans attach to the right parent. It's fragile because the context must survive function calls, threads, and async tasks; contextvars don't automatically flow into new threads, and a missed hop makes child spans orphan into parentless roots — silently, with no error, breaking the tree and the cost/latency roll-ups.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The mechanism that carries the parent-span reference across execution boundaries so the trace tree nests correctly.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Spans have no inherent link to their caller; without an explicitly propagated context, each new span can't know which span invoked it.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The active span is stored in a contextvars.ContextVar; new spans read it as parent. Across threads you copy the context (copy_context + ctx.run); across async the event loop preserves it, but manual task spawning may require re-binding.

theory.whyImportant: It's the difference between a readable tree with correct roll-ups and a pile of orphaned spans that misattribute cost and latency, and it fails silently, so it's the top source of real tracing bugs.
theory.realWorldExample: Tool calls fanned out onto worker threads showed up as separate root traces until the team wrapped each worker with copy_context().run, which re-nested them under the planner span.

followUps.question: Why not store the parent in a global variable?
followUps.answer: A global breaks under concurrency — interleaved runs and threads would clobber each other's parent; contextvars are per-context and safe to copy across boundaries.

followUps.question: How do you detect orphaned spans early?
followUps.answer: Assert parent links in tests and add a monitor that flags traces with unexpected root spans, so a propagation regression surfaces before roll-ups look wrong.

scenario.question: Your team is on LangSmith today but leadership wants the option to move to Langfuse or self-hosted OpenTelemetry later without a painful migration. How do you instrument the agent now to keep that door open?
scenario.directAnswer: Depend on your own thin tracing interface, not the vendor SDK. Define a Tracer with span(name, **attrs) and the durable concepts (trace, span, parent context, attributes), implement it against LangSmith today, and keep all vendor calls inside that adapter. App code opens spans through your interface, so switching to Langfuse or OTel means rewriting one adapter, not every call site.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A vendor-abstraction strategy that isolates SDK-specific code behind a stable, concept-based interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Observability SDKs churn and vendors get swapped, but the primitives (span, trace, parent/child, attributes) are identical across all of them.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You model the durable concepts in your own Tracer, route context propagation and attribute recording through it, and implement the backend once; a migration re-implements the adapter against the new SDK while call sites stay untouched.

scenario.whyImportant: It converts a potential multi-week rewrite into a contained, testable change, and it keeps your instrumentation aligned with concepts that outlive any single tool.
scenario.realWorldExample: A team behind a Tracer adapter moved from a hosted SDK to self-hosted OTel by rewriting only the adapter and its exporter; the hundreds of span() call sites in the agent never changed.

followUps.question: What belongs in the adapter vs the app?
followUps.answer: The adapter owns SDK clients, exporters, and context wiring; the app owns only span names, boundaries, and business attributes expressed through your interface.

followUps.question: How do you avoid the adapter leaking vendor concepts?
followUps.answer: Keep its surface to the durable primitives — span, attributes, parent context — and refuse to expose vendor-specific types so callers can't couple to them.

coding.question: Implement a context-manager span() that nests spans into a trace tree using contextvars, recording each span's parent correctly.
coding.thoughtProcess: The tree is built by having each new span read the currently-active span as its parent, then make itself active for the duration of its body, then restore the previous active span on exit so siblings get the right parent. contextvars.ContextVar plus the token from set()/reset() gives exactly that save-and-restore behavior, and it's concurrency-safe unlike a global.

solution.code:
import contextvars
from contextlib import contextmanager

_current = contextvars.ContextVar("current", default=None)
spans = []

@contextmanager
def span(name, **attrs):
    parent = _current.get()                         # active span = parent
    rec = {"name": name,
           "parent": parent["name"] if parent else None,
           "attrs": attrs}
    spans.append(rec)
    token = _current.set(rec)                        # become the parent
    try:
        yield rec
    finally:
        _current.reset(token)                        # restore for siblings

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with span("agent.run"):
        with span("llm.plan"):
            with span("tool.search", tokens=120):
                pass
        with span("llm.answer"):
            pass
    for s in spans:
        print(s["name"], "parent=", s["parent"])

lineByLine: A module-level ContextVar holds the currently-active span; its default None marks the root.
On entry, span() reads the active span as its parent before creating its own record.
The record stores the parent's name and any attributes, then is appended in creation order.
_current.set(rec) makes this span the active parent and returns a token for later restoration.
Inside the try, nested spans opened in the body will read this span as their parent.
The finally block calls _current.reset(token) so the previous active span is restored, giving siblings the correct parent instead of this one.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) per span open/close; O(n) total for n spans in a run.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) to retain the n span records; O(d) context-var depth for nesting depth d.

followUps.question: How would you make this work across worker threads?
followUps.answer: Capture contextvars.copy_context() on the parent and run each worker via ctx.run, so the ContextVar resolves to the real parent instead of the thread's default.

followUps.question: How would you record latency per span?
followUps.answer: Stamp time.perf_counter() on entry and compute the delta in the finally block, storing it as an attribute alongside tokens and cost.

keyTakeaways: A span is one recorded operation (LLM/tool call) with inputs, outputs, tokens, latency, and cost; a trace is the tree of a whole run.
The trace tree mirrors control flow, letting you read top-down what the agent decided and where time and money went.
Context propagation links each span to its parent; miss it across a thread/async boundary and child spans orphan silently.
Attributes (tokens, latency, cost, tags) are what you aggregate to find slow, expensive, or failing steps.
LangSmith, Langfuse, and OTel share the same concepts; hide the SDK behind a thin adapter so vendor churn is a one-file edit.
